claims.statement: IMDT members agree to actively provide and promote force-free training methods and reject methods or equipment that may cause physical or mental discomfort.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Paraphrase of published ethics bullets on imdt.uk.com/code-of-ethics.
limitations: Applies to IMDT members, not all UK trainers.

claims.statement: IMDT members agree to avoid positive punishment and negative reinforcement as tools for training dogs.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Ethics text states members avoid positive punishment and negative reinforcement as training tools.
limitations: Organisational norm; not identical to all scientific operational definitions of +/-R and +/-P.

claims.statement: IMDT members agree to work within professional limits and refer owners to a suitable professional when needs exceed those limits.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Ethics requires referral when owner needs are beyond member competence.

claims.statement: In the UK, animal trainers, training instructors and behaviourists are not regulated by government; anyone may use those job titles regardless of training or experience.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: ABTC states UK trainers/behaviourists are not government-regulated.
limitations: Legal context may change; requires periodic re-verification against official sources.

claims.statement: ABTC requires registered trainers, instructors and behaviourists to use science-based methods and keep up to date with research-informed thinking.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: ABTC describes science-based methods and continuing alignment with research.
claims.confidenceJustification: ABTC council position for registered practitioners.
limitations: Applies to ABTC-registered practitioners via member organisations, not all trainers.

claims.statement: ABTC states it does not agree with aversives being used to train animals and publishes an indicative list of aversive equipment and methods that should not be used.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Page states ABTC does not agree with aversives for training; list is non-exhaustive.
claims.confidenceJustification: Clear position statement; detailed list not yet extracted into separate claims in batch 001.
limitations: Full equipment list pending extraction from ABTC ethical training leaflet.

claims.statement: Positive reinforcement training means giving the dog something they want when they behave in a way the owner likes, making that behaviour more likely in future.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Dogs Trust defines reward-based training as giving desired outcomes for liked behaviours.
claims.confidenceJustification: Consistent with operant conditioning definitions; charity educational standard.

claims.statement: When starting a new skill, Dogs Trust advises rewarding the dog every time they are successful; reward type and schedule can change after the behaviour is reliable across environments.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Guidance to reward every success initially, then vary rewards after generalisation.
limitations: Does not specify numeric session lengths or repetition counts.

claims.statement: A marker signal must always be followed by a reward so the dog can be confident they got the behaviour right.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Marker means yes, reward is coming; must be followed by reward.
claims.confidenceJustification: Standard marker-training mechanics repeated across charities.

claims.statement: Undesired behaviour may increase if the dog receives attention, eye contact or interaction as a consequence—even when the owner intends to discourage the behaviour.
claims.locator: What if your dog is behaving undesirably?
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Example given: jumping up met with verbal and physical interaction may reward jumping.
claims.confidenceJustification: Mechanism aligns with operant learning; illustrated by single scenario.
limitations: Illustrative example; not quantified across populations.

claims.statement: Before training new behaviours, the dog should learn that the marker predicts a reward via repeated marker-then-treat pairings.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Repeat marker then treat several times until dog expects treat after marker.
claims.confidenceJustification: Standard classical conditioning setup for marker.
limitations: Does not specify exact number of pairings.

claims.statement: Dogs Trust advises saying a verbal marker as calmly as possible because excited delivery can excite, confuse or distract the dog.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Calm, consistent tone for marker words.
claims.confidenceJustification: Practical guidance; individual dogs may differ.

claims.statement: Dogs Trust advises teaching reliable name response before adding a formal recall cue.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Get attention using name before recall cue.

claims.statement: Dogs Trust advises giving the dog at least five seconds to respond to a recall cue before calling again, and not repeating the cue if the dog is unlikely to return.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Five-second wait; avoid repeated cues that teach ignoring.
limitations: Five seconds is charity guidance, not a universal research-derived constant.

claims.statement: If a dog ignores recall during training, Dogs Trust advises staying calm because anger or shouting can reduce willingness to return; use long line guidance or collect the dog instead of punishing.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Stay calm; gently guide with long line; never pull dog toward you.

claims.statement: Dogs Trust advises off-lead exercise in open spaces only when the owner is confident the dog will come back when called.
claims.locator: What to do if your dog keeps running away
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Off lead only when recall reliable; otherwise long line and secure areas.
limitations: Reliability threshold not numerically defined by source.

claims.statement: Dogs Trust states that in the UK dogs in public should wear a collar and ID tag and have up-to-date microchip details, as required by law.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Collar, ID tag, microchip compliance referenced as UK law.
claims.confidenceJustification: Charity summary aligns with GOV.UK and Control of Dogs Order 1992; see claim-govuk-002 and claim-cdo1992-001 in batch 003.
limitations: Devolved rules for cats/microchip differ; this claim concerns dogs in public.

claims.statement: RSPCA states all dog training should be reward based, using food, toys or praise when the dog shows desired behaviour.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: All training should be reward based.

claims.statement: RSPCA recommends breaking training into short but regular sessions and starting new tricks in a quiet room with minimal distractions.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Short regular sessions; quiet starting environment.
limitations: No specific duration in minutes given.

claims.statement: RSPCA recommends looking for ABTC-registered animal training instructors for ethical training that meets welfare needs.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: ABTC-registered instructors assessed for skills to support ethical training.

claims.statement: RSPCA advises owners not to join classes if techniques rely on fear, pain, choke chains, shouting or hitting.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Avoid fear, pain, choke chains, shouting, hitting.
claims.confidenceJustification: Explicit welfare filter for class selection.

claims.statement: RSPCA advises adding the verbal cue 'sit' only as the dog moves into sit, not before, to avoid associating the word with the wrong movement.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Add cue word as dog sits, not before movement.

claims.statement: In a 2004 owner survey (n=364), owner-rated obedience across eight tasks correlated positively with the number of tasks trained using rewards (P<0.01) but not with tasks trained using punishment (P=0.5).
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Abstract reports correlation with reward use, not punishment use, for obedience ratings.
claims.confidenceJustification: Peer-reviewed but correlational owner reports from 2004.
limitations: Correlational; obedience self-rated; mixed training methods common.

claims.statement: In Hiby et al. (2004), the number of owner-reported problem behaviours correlated with the number of tasks trained using punishment (P<0.001) but not with tasks trained using rewards (P=0.17).
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Abstract links punishment use with more reported problems.
claims.confidenceJustification: Peer-reviewed survey; problem behaviours and training history both owner-reported.
limitations: Cannot infer causation; problem behaviour list not validated in this KB extraction.

claims.statement: Hiby et al. (2004) conclude that punishment may represent a welfare concern without concurrent benefits in obedience within the pet-owning community surveyed.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Authors conclude punishment associated with welfare concerns without obedience benefits in sample.
claims.confidenceJustification: Author interpretation grounded in correlational data.
limitations: Single study; dated; pet owner population.

claims.statement: Hiby et al. (2004) note that although their survey did not support punishment-based methods for pet owners, they are not claiming punishment cannot be used effectively, citing historical successful use in some training contexts.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Authors acknowledge historical effective punishment use but emphasise inexperienced pet owners.
limitations: Does not endorse punishment for Good Dog; records scientific nuance only.

claims.statement: If a dog does not always come when called, Dogs Trust advises keeping them on a long line or lead rather than relying on off-lead freedom.
claims.excerptOrParaphrase: Long line or lead when recall not reliable.
